definition: Language identification in the limit is a formal model for inductive inference of formal languages, mainly by computers (see machine learning and induction of regular languages).
details: It was introduced by E. Mark Gold in a technical report and a journal article with the same title. In this model, a teacher provides to a learner some presentation (i.e. a sequence of strings) of some formal language. The learning is seen as an infinite process. Each time the learner reads an element of the presentation, it should provide a representation (e.g. a formal grammar) for the language. Gold defines that a learner can identify in the limit a class of languages if, given any presentation of any language in the class, the learner will produce only a finite number of wrong representations, and then stick with the correct representation. However, the learner need not be able to announce its correctness; and the teacher might present a counterexample to any representation arbitrarily long after. Gold defined two types of presentations: Text (positive information): an enumeration of all strings the language consists of. Complete presentation (positive and negative information): an enumeration of all possible strings, each with a label indicating if the string belongs to the language or not.

explainer.lead: Language identification in the limit is a formal model of how a learner can infer a formal language from a never-ending stream of examples. It matters because it gives precise conditions under which inductive inference succeeds.

tiers.eli5: Imagine guessing the rule behind a list of words as more words keep arriving — the question is whether you eventually settle on the right rule and stay there.
tiers.practitioner: The model defines learning as an infinite process in which the learner outputs a representation after each new element. The pitfall is that identifying in the limit says nothing about how fast or how confidently the learner converges.
tiers.paperLevel: Introduced by E. Mark Gold in a technical report and a journal article of the same title. A teacher provides a presentation (a sequence of strings) of a formal language; after reading each element the learner provides a representation, such as a formal grammar. A learner can identify in the limit a class of languages if, given any presentation, it converges to a correct representation.

explainer.example: A learner reads a growing sequence of strings and after each one proposes a grammar, eventually settling on the correct one.
